claim: The MNV and the prototype HuNoV Norwalk virus (NV) VPg proteins are covalently linked to the viral genome via the highly conserved tyrosine residue within an N-terminal DEEYD/E motif found in all calicivirus VPg proteins.
source: The MNV and the prototype HuNoV Norwalk virus (NV) VPg proteins are covalently linked to the viral genome via the highly conserved tyrosine residue within an N-terminal DEEYD/E motif found in all calicivirus VPg proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A which shows the amino acid sequence alignment highlighting the conserved tyrosine residue.

claim: The norovirus VPg proteins contain a highly conserved C-terminal domain which is necessary and sufficient for binding to the translation initiation factor eIF4G via an interaction that requires a highly conserved phenylalanine residue.
source: In addition, the norovirus VPg proteins contain a highly conserved C-terminal domain which we have shown to be necessary and sufficient for binding to the translation initiation factor eIF4G via an interaction that requires a highly conserved phenylalanine residue (Figure 1A) (Chung et al., 2014; Leen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chung et al., 2014; Leen et al., 2016) and reference to Figure 1A showing the conserved phenylalanine residue.

claim: The NV VPg protein, as produced during authentic virus replication in a NV replicon bearing cell line, interacts with the cap-binding complex eIF4F.
source: Using affinity purification on m7-GTP sepharose, we confirmed that the NV VPg protein, as produced during authentic virus replication in a NV replicon bearing cell line, interacts with the cap-binding complex eIF4F (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from affinity purification shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Components of the eIF4F complex, namely the eIF4E cap-binding protein, the eIF4A helicase and the eIF4GI scaffold protein, along with poly-A binding protein (PABP) and eIF3 subunits, were readily purified on m7-GTP sepharose.
source: Components of the eIF4F complex, namely the eIF4E cap-binding protein, the eIF4A helicase and the eIF4GI scaffold protein, along with poly-A binding protein (PABP) and eIF3 subunits, were readily purified on m7-GTP sepharose, whereas GAPDH was not.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from affinity purification experiments.

claim: In NV-replicon containing cells, mature VPg was enriched on m7-GTP sepharose but the NS3 protein was not.
source: In NV-replicon containing cells, mature VPg was also enriched on m7-GTP sepharose but the NS3 protein, known to have RNA binding and helicase activity (Li et al., 2018), was not.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from affinity purification and cites previous work on NS3 function.

claim: Transfection of GFP-tagged versions of either the MNV or NV VPg proteins into 293 T cells allowed for the affinity purification of eIF4F components.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that transfection of GFP-tagged versions of either the MNV or NV VPg proteins into 293 T cells allowed for the affinity purification of eIF4F components and that mutations in the eIF4G binding domain of VPg reduced this association (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mutations in the eIF4G binding domain of VPg reduced the association with eIF4F components.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that transfection of GFP-tagged versions of either the MNV or NV VPg proteins into 293 T cells allowed for the affinity purification of eIF4F components and that mutations in the eIF4G binding domain of VPg reduced this association (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C comparing wild-type and mutant VPg proteins.

claim: Most of the proteins identified by quantitative mass spectrometry of VPg-associated complexes were components of the host cell translation complex including ribosomal proteins, translation initiation factors and host RNA binding proteins.
source: Most of the proteins identified were components of the host cell translation complex including ribosomal proteins, translation initiation factors and host RNA binding proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data presented in Figure 1D and supplementary files.

claim: hnRNPA1 was identified in VPg-associated complexes and has been previously shown to act in norovirus genome circularization.
source: In addition, we identified hnRNPA1 which we have previously shown to act in norovirus genome circularization (López-Manríquez et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on hnRNPA1 function.

claim: YBX1, DDX3 and several other proteins that previously interact with the 5' end of the viral RNA were enriched on VPg.
source: YBX1, DDX3 and several other proteins that we have previously found to interact with the 5' end of the viral RNA (Vashist et al., 2012a) were also enriched on VPg (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on 5' RNA binding proteins.

claim: The association of all proteins tested except YBX1 were reduced by the introduction of eIF4G-binding site mutations into the MNV VPg protein.
source: Except for YBX1, the association of all proteins tested were reduced by the introduction of eIF4G-binding site mutations into the MNV VPg protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The norovirus VPg proteins interact with a complex network of host factors, many of which have been implicated in the host cell translation initiation process.
source: Together, these data extend our previous observations and confirm that the norovirus VPg proteins interact with a complex network of host factors, many of which have been implicated in the host cell translation initiation process.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined proteomic and western blot data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Silver stain of the purified complexes from FLAG-tagged virus infections confirmed the presence of the bait proteins, with both the uncleaved and cleaved forms of NS1/2 and NS2 being highly enriched.
source: Silver stain of the purified complexes confirmed the presence of the bait proteins, with both the uncleaved and cleaved forms of NS1/2 and NS2 being highly enriched (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by silver stain data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Complexes purified from NS1/2-Flag virus infected cells co-purified untagged NS4 and vice versa.
source: As expected, complexes purified from NS1/2-Flag virus infected cells co-purified untagged NS4 and vice versa (Figure 2B), as we have previously shown these proteins to interact to form a complex (Thorne et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by silver stain data in Figure 2B and cites previous work on NS1/2-NS4 interaction.

claim: Western blot analysis of the purified complexes confirmed that viral non-structural and structural proteins were specifically enriched in the purified complexes, including NS5 (VPg)-containing precursors.
source: Western blot analysis of the purified complexes confirmed that viral non-structural and structural proteins were specifically enriched in the purified complexes, including NS5 (VPg)-containing precursors (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All viral proteins, including the VF1 protein product of ORF4, were enriched in the viral replication complex.
source: As expected, all viral proteins, including the VF1 protein product of ORF4, an innate immune antagonist (McFadden et al., 2011), were enriched in the viral replication complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on VF1 function.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the relative enrichment of proteins identified using NS1/2 and NS4 (Spearman correlation of 0.8832).
source: There was a significant correlation between the relative enrichment of proteins identified using NS1/2 and NS4 (Spearman correlation of 0.8832), fitting with our prior knowledge that both proteins form a complex during viral replication (Thorne et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on NS1/2-NS4 complex formation.

claim: Ontology analysis indicated that proteins involved in vesicle transport and fatty acid metabolism were significantly enriched in the replication complex.
source: Ontology analysis indicated that proteins involved in vesicle transport and fatty acid metabolism were significantly enriched (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3), fitting with previous observations that the viral replication complex is associated with cytoplasmic membranous structures (Cotton et al., 2017; Hyde and Mackenzie, 2010; Hyde et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on replication complex membrane association.

claim: VapA and the paralogue VapB, which bind to the NS1/2 protein, were both highly enriched in the replication complex.
source: We noted that the VapA and the paralogue VapB, which we have recently identified as binding to the NS1/2 protein (McCune et al., 2017), were both highly enriched.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on VapA/VapB-NS1/2 interaction.

claim: NS4 failed to enrich mature VPg, instead purifying only the polyprotein cleavage intermediate NS4/5(VPg).
source: We observed that NS4 failed to enrich mature VPg, instead purifying only the polyprotein cleavage intermediate NS4/5(VPg) (Figure 2C and S2.2).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: NS1/2 effectively pulled down mature VPg.
source: In contrast, NS1/2 effectively pulled down mature VPg (Figure 2C and S2.2).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: NS1/2 enriched the VPg binding partner eIF4G more than 2-fold, while pulldown of NS4 resulted in no eIF4G enrichment.
source: Consistent with this, NS1/2 enriched the VPg binding partner eIF4G more than 2-fold, while pulldown of NS4 resulted in no eIF4G enrichment, likely indicating that the NS4/5 (VPg) precursor cannot effectively function in translation initiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The NS4/5 (VPg) precursor cannot effectively function in translation initiation.
source: Consistent with this, NS1/2 enriched the VPg binding partner eIF4G more than 2-fold, while pulldown of NS4 resulted in no eIF4G enrichment, likely indicating that the NS4/5 (VPg) precursor cannot effectively function in translation initiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that NS4/5(VPg) does not enrich eIF4G, combined with knowledge that eIF4G binding is required for VPg-dependent translation.

claim: Binding of C-terminal VPg fusion proteins to eIF4G is inhibited.
source: This is consistent with a previous observation that binding of C-terminal VPg fusion proteins to eIF4G is inhibited (Leen et al., 2016), but may further suggest that the function of VPg is also altered when present as an N-terminal fusion with NS4.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Leen et al., 2016).

claim: Most host factors identified using VPg were enriched by >2 fold using only the NS1/2 tagged virus, and not the NS4-tagged virus.
source: Consistent with our observations with the well-established VPg partner eIF4G, most host factors identified using VPg were enriched by >2 fold using only the NS1/2 tagged virus, and not the NS4-tagged virus.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of mass spectrometry data from VPg, NS1/2, and NS4 pulldowns.

claim: G3BP1 was enriched by VPg, NS1/2, and NS4.
source: One protein was enriched by VPg, NS1/2, and NS4 – the core stress granule protein G3BP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the CRISPR screen, the MNV receptor Cd300lf was the most highly positively selected gene identified.
source: In both screens, the MNV receptor Cd300lf was the most highly positively selected gene identified, in agreement with previous reports (Haga et al., 2016; Orchard et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR screen data and cites previous reports identifying Cd300lf as the MNV receptor.

claim: The previously characterised pro-viral MNV gene VapA was identified in both CRISPR screens.
source: The previously characterised pro-viral MNV gene VapA (McCune et al., 2017) was also identified in both screens (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR screen data and cites previous work characterizing VapA.

claim: G3BP1 was the second most highly enriched gene in the CRISPR screen.
source: The second most highly enriched gene was G3BP1, a gene also identified in one of the two previous CRISPR screens performed on norovirus infected cells (Orchard et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR screen data and cites a previous CRISPR screen.

claim: Comparing the CRISPR data obtained using two divergent strains of MNV showed 89 common pro-viral hits and five common anti-viral hits.
source: Comparing the CRISPR data obtained in this study using two divergent strains of MNV showed a high degree of overlap, with 89 common pro-viral hit and five common anti-viral hits (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of CRISPR screen data from CW3 and CR6 strains.

claim: Four genes were identified as common proviral hits across all CRISPR screens: CD300lf, G3BP1, Kmt2d, and Smarce1.
source: However comparison with the previous reported CRISPR screen used to identify the MNV receptor (Orchard et al., 2016) showed only seven proviral hits for CW3 and 8 for CR6, of which only four were common for both strains across all screens (Supplementary file 4). The four genes identified were the MNV receptor CD300lf, the stress granule component G3BP1, the histone methytransferase Kmt2d and Smarce1, which encodes an actin dependent regulator of chromatin.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of CRISPR screen data across multiple studies.

claim: Pathway over-representation analysis of the pro-viral genes identified in the CRISPR screens highlighted mRNA processing, RNA splicing and methylation as the three most highly represented gene ontology terms.
source: Pathway over-representation analysis (Liao et al., 2019) of the genes pro-viral genes identified in the CRISPR screens performed in this study highlighted mRNA processing, RNA splicing and methylation as the three most highly represented gene ontology (GO) terms (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of CRISPR screen data.

claim: PTBP1 was one of the genes identified in the enriched GO terms and has been previously shown to bind to a 3' pyrimidine-rich stretch in the MNV genome which is important for viral pathogenesis.
source: The gene encoding PTBP1, polypyrimidine tract binding protein, was one of the genes identified in these enriched GO terms. PTBP1 is a protein we have previously shown to bind to a 3' pyrimidine-rich stretch in the MNV genome which is important for viral pathogenesis (Bailey et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR screen data and cites previous work on PTBP1 function.

claim: G3BP1 was identified in all three screens (VPg proteomics, replication complex proteomics, and CRISPR) as a potential host factor essential for norovirus infection.
source: A cross-comparison of the data obtained from all three approaches allowed us to identify several host proteins that were common to all screens (Supplementary file 5). G3BP1, the core stress granule component was identified in all three screens as a potential host factor essential for norovirus infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data from all three experimental approaches.

claim: A clear defect was observed in the ability to replicate and produce infectious virus in three independently selected ΔG3BP1 cell lines.
source: A clear defect was observed in the ability to replicate to produce infectious virus in three independently selected ΔG3BP1 cell lines (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The inability of MNV to replicate in ΔG3BP1 cells was mirrored by an inability to induce cytopathic effect leading to virus-induced cell death.
source: This effect was mirrored by an inability to induce cytopathic effect leading to virus-induced cell death (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytopathic effect data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The ability of encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) to infect and cause cell death was unaffected by the deletion of G3BP1.
source: In contrast, the ability of encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) to infect and cause cell death was unaffected by the deletion of G3BP1 (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytopathic effect data shown in Figure 4C and D comparing MNV and EMCV infection.

claim: Cells lacking G3BP1 are highly resistant to norovirus infection.
source: These data confirm that cells lacking G3BP1 are highly resistant to norovirus infection.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing defects in MNV replication and cytopathic effect in ΔG3BP1 cells.

claim: Transfection of replicon RNA, purified from replicon containing cells, into BHK cells readily resulted in the formation of antibiotic resistant cell colonies.
source: Transfection of replicon RNA, purified from replicon containing cells, into BHK cells readily resulted in the formation of antibiotic resistant cell colonies (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RNA that was proteinase K treated prior to transfection was unable to produce replicon containing colonies.
source: In contrast, RNA that was proteinase K treated prior to transfection was unable to produce replicon containing colonies.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5A comparing untreated and proteinase K treated RNA.

claim: CRISPR modified U2OS cells that lacked G3BP1 were unable to support NV replication, as evident by the lack of antibiotic resistant colonies.
source: CRISPR modified U2OS cells that lacked G3BP1 (Kedersha et al., 2016) were unable to support NV replication, as evident by the lack of antibiotic resistant colonies (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5B and cites the source of the G3BP1 knockout cells.

claim: While a significant increase in NV viral RNA levels was seen in WT U2OS cells, those lacking G3BP1 were completely unable to support NV RNA synthesis.
source: While a significant increase in NV viral RNA levels was seen in WT U2OS cells, those lacking G3BP1 were completely unable to support NV RNA synthesis (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the absence of G3BP1 the formation of antibiotic resistant microcolonies was completely ablated and then subsequently restored in ΔG3BP1 cells engineered to express the wild type version of G3BP1.
source: In the absence of G3BP1 the formation of antibiotic resistant microcolonies was completely ablated and then subsequently restored in ΔG3BP1 cells engineered to express the wild type version of G3BP1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5D comparing WT, ΔG3BP1, and complemented cells.

claim: G3BP1 is essential for human Norwalk virus replication.
source: These data indicate that like for MNV, G3BP1 is essential for human Norwalk virus replication.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing defects in NV replication in G3BP1 knockout cells.

claim: Complementation with full length murine G3BP1 restored the ability of MNV to induce cell death back to near wild type levels.
source: Complementation with full length murine G3BP1 restored the ability of MNV to induce cell death (Figure 6B) and to produce infectious virus (Figure 6C) back to near wild type levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by cytopathic effect and virus yield data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Complementation with a variant carrying a deletion of the RGG domain resulted in limited complementation.
source: In contrast, complementation with a variant carrying a deletion of the RGG domain resulted in limited complementation, and deletion of both the RGG and RRM domains together resulted in complete loss of complementation capacity (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytopathic effect and virus yield data shown in Figure 6B and 6C comparing different G3BP1 truncations.

claim: Deletion of both the RGG and RRM domains together resulted in complete loss of complementation capacity.
source: In contrast, complementation with a variant carrying a deletion of the RGG domain resulted in limited complementation, and deletion of both the RGG and RRM domains together resulted in complete loss of complementation capacity (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytopathic effect and virus yield data shown in Figure 6B and 6C comparing different G3BP1 truncations.

claim: The RNA binding domains of G3BP1 are essential for its function in the norovirus life cycle.
source: These data confirm that the RNA binding domains of G3BP1 are essential for its function in the norovirus life cycle.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the complementation experiments showing that deletion of RNA binding domains abolishes G3BP1 function.

claim: The levels of infectivity obtained following transfection of ΔG3BP1 cell lines with MNV viral RNA was comparable to that obtained in WT cells in the presence of the nucleoside analogue 2'-C-methylcytidin (2CMC).
source: The levels of infectivity obtained following transfection of ΔG3BP1 cell lines with MNV viral RNA was comparable to that obtained in WT cells in the presence of the nucleoside analogue 2'-C-methylcytidin (2CMC), a known inhibitor of the norovirus RNA polymerase (Rocha-Pereira et al., 2012; Rocha-Pereira et al., 2013) (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by virus yield data shown in Figure 7A and cites previous work on 2CMC as a polymerase inhibitor.

claim: No viral proteins were detected in either of the ΔG3BP1 cell lines following transfection of VPg-linked RNA, suggesting a defect at a very early stage in the viral life cycle.
source: No viral proteins were detected in either of the ΔG3BP1 cell lines suggesting a defect at a very early stage in the viral life cycle (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C and represents an inference about the stage of the life cycle affected.

claim: Transfection of VPg-linked RNA into the ΔG3BP1 cell lines reconstituted with WT G3BP1 restored the ability to produce infectious virus and viral proteins.
source: Transfection of VPg-linked RNA into the ΔG3BP1 cell lines reconstituted with WT G3BP1 restored the ability to produce infectious virus (Figure 7B) and the production of viral proteins (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by virus yield and western blot data shown in Figure 7B and 7D.

claim: G3BP1 is required for a post entry stage of the norovirus life cycle.
source: These data confirm that G3BP1 is required for a post entry stage of the norovirus life cycle and that in the absence of G3BP1 no norovirus replication was observed within the sensitivity of the assay used.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from RNA transfection experiments that bypass the entry step.

claim: In the absence of G3BP1 no norovirus replication was observed within the sensitivity of the assay used.
source: These data confirm that G3BP1 is required for a post entry stage of the norovirus life cycle and that in the absence of G3BP1 no norovirus replication was observed within the sensitivity of the assay used.
evidence: The claim is supported by the lack of detectable viral proteins and infectious virus in ΔG3BP1 cells.

claim: The production of viral positive sense RNA was reduced to background levels in the absence of G3BP1, comparable to levels observed when 2CMC was present during the infection.
source: The production of viral positive sense RNA was reduced to background levels in the absence of G3BP1, comparable to levels observed when the 2CMC was present during the infection (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by strand-specific RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Viral negative sense RNA synthesis was reduced to below the detection limit of the assay in ΔG3BP1 cell lines.
source: Viral negative sense RNA synthesis was also reduced to below the detection limit of the assay in ΔG3BP1 cell lines (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by strand-specific RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: An ~5 fold increase in viral negative sense RNA production was detected at 6 hr post infection of WT cells in the presence of 2CMC, likely representing the first round of viral negative sense RNA synthesis.
source: Surprisingly, we were able to detect an ~5 fold increase in viral negative sense RNA production at 6 hr post infection of WT cells in the presence of 2CMC, which, given that 2CMC was added after the inoculation phase (Figure 8B), likely represents the first round of viral negative sense RNA synthesis, confirming the sensitivity of the assay.
evidence: The claim is supported by strand-specific RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8C and represents an interpretation of the data.

claim: Viral positive and negative sense RNA synthesis was near (or below) the sensitivity of the assay following transfection of viral VPg-linked RNA into two independent ΔG3BP1 cell lines.
source: Similar results were obtained following transfection of viral RNA into cells to bypass the entry phase; viral positive and negative sense RNA synthesis was near (or below) the sensitivity of the assay following transfection of viral VPg-linked RNA into two independent ΔG3BP1 cell lines (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by strand-specific RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: Complementation with WT G3BP1, but not the mutant forms lacking the RNA binding domains, restored viral positive and negative sense RNA synthesis.
source: Complementation with WT G3BP1, but not the mutant forms lacking the RNA binding domains, also restored viral positive and negative sense RNA synthesis (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by strand-specific RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8F and G comparing complementation with different G3BP1 variants.

claim: The function of G3BP1 is prior to, or at the level of viral negative sense RNA synthesis.
source: Together these data suggest that the function of G3BP1 is prior to, or at the level of viral negative sense RNA synthesis, with the most logical steps being either viral RNA translation or the formation of viral replication complexes.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the RNA synthesis data showing defects at the level of negative strand synthesis.

claim: The norovirus VPg proteins form a complex that contains multiple components of the large and small ribosomal subunits.
source: Our proteomics analysis also confirms that the norovirus VPg proteins form a complex that contains multiple components of the large and small ribosomal subunits (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: G3BP1 associates with 40S subunits.
source: It has been established previously that G3BP1 associates with 40S subunits (Kedersha et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: GFP-tagged WT MNV VPg was readily able to pull down eIF4G, G3BP1 and RpS6, a component of the 40S subunit.
source: GFP-tagged WT MNV VPg was readily able to pull down eIF4G, G3BP1 and RpS6, a component of the 40S subunit (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-Trap immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: In the absence of G3BP1, the ability to pull down RpS6 and RpS3 was lost.
source: However, in the absence of G3BP1, the ability to pull down RpS6 and RpS3 was lost (Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-Trap immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Disruption of the VPg-eIF4G interaction by the introduction of the F123A mutation significantly reduced the ability to pull down RpS6, RpS3, and RpL4.
source: Furthermore, we found that disruption of the VPg-eIF4G interaction by the introduction of the F123A mutation into the eIF4G binding domain, also significantly reduced the ability to pull down RpS6, RpS3, as well as RpL4, a component of the large ribosomal subunit (Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-Trap immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upon reconstitution of G3BP1 expression, the levels of RpS6, RpS3 and RpL4 associated with VPg were enhanced.
source: We also observed that upon reconstitution of G3BP1 expression, the levels of RpS6, RpS3 and RpL4 associated with VPg were enhanced (Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-Trap immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of G3BP1, the amount of viral RNA associated with the ribosomal subunit protein RpS3 was decreased.
source: We found that in the absence of G3BP1, the amount of viral RNA associated with the ribosomal subunit protein RpS3 was decreased (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-IP data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: G3BP1 likely contributes in some manner to the association of VPg and viral VPg-linked RNA with ribosomal subunits.
source: These data suggest that that G3BP1 likely contributes in some manner to the association of VPg and viral VPg-linked RNA with ribosomal subunits.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the GFP-Trap and RNA-IP data showing reduced ribosome association in the absence of G3BP1.

claim: Even in the presence of 2CMC, which inhibits viral RNA synthesis, there was a small but measurable increase in free 80S ribosomes over time in WT cells but not in cells lacking G3BP1.
source: We noted that even in the presence of 2CMC, which inhibits viral RNA synthesis, there was a small but measurable increase in free 80S ribosomes over time in WT cells but not in cells lacking G3BP1 (Figure 10A).
evidence: The claim is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: MNV infection results in translation shut off and this effect is at least partially due to the activity of the NS6 protease.
source: We have previously found that MNV infection results in translation shut off and that this effect is at least partially due to the activity of the NS6 protease (Emmott et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: While most ribosome-associated norovirus RNA in WT cells was found in polysomes containing fractions, less viral RNA was found in ribosome-containing fractions in the absence of G3BP1.
source: Further analyses indicated that while most ribosome-associated norovirus RNA in WT cells was found in polysomes containing fractions, less viral RNA was found in ribosome-containing fractions (1–12 in Figure 10A and B) in the absence of G3BP1 and, in comparison to WT cells, very little viral RNA was found in fractions containing polysomes (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by polysome profiling and viral RNA quantification data shown in Figure 10A and B.

claim: In the absence of G3BP1 norovirus RNA is less efficient at assembling into polysomal fractions, suggesting a defect at the level of viral protein synthesis.
source: Extending the fractionation to include the free RNA and ribonucleoprotein complexes at the top of each gradient confirmed that in the absence of G3BP1 norovirus RNA is less efficient at assembling into polysomal fractions, suggesting a defect at the level of viral protein synthesis (Figure 10C).
evidence: The claim is supported by extended polysome profiling data shown in Figure 10C and represents an interpretation of the data.

claim: G3BP1 functions to promote the translation of norovirus VPg-linked RNA, by facilitating the association with ribosomal subunits and the formation of polysomes on viral RNA.
source: Together these data support the hypothesis that G3BP1 functions to promote the translation of norovirus VPg-linked RNA, by facilitating the association with ribosomal subunits and the formation of polysomes on viral RNA.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the polysome profiling data showing reduced polysome association in the absence of G3BP1.

claim: Both cap-dependent and CrPV IRES-dependent translation were comparable in extracts prepared from WT and ΔG3BP1 cell lines.
source: Both cap-dependent (Figure 11B) and CrPV IRES-dependent translation (Figure 11C) were comparable in extracts prepared from WT and ΔG3BP1 cell lines (Figure 11A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro translation data shown in Figure 11B and C.

claim: Norovirus VPg-dependent translation was reduced in nuclease treated extracts prepared from cells lacking G3BP.
source: We found that norovirus VPg-dependent translation was reduced in nuclease treated extracts prepared from cells lacking G3BP (Figure 11D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro translation data shown in Figure 11D.

claim: Translation in nuclease treated extracts was on average reduced by ~40–50% because of G3BP1 ablation.
source: Quantification of the levels of multiple viral proteins produced over multiple experiments indicated that translation in nuclease treated extracts was on average reduced by ~40–50% because of G3BP1 ablation (Figure 11E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of in vitro translation data shown in Figure 11E.

claim: A 50% reduction in translation efficiency was consistently observed in extracts that were not nuclease treated, and therefore contained physiologically relevant levels of cellular mRNAs.
source: This 50% reduction in translation efficiency was also consistently observed in extracts that were not nuclease treated, and therefore contained physiologically relevant levels of cellular mRNAs (Figure 11F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro translation data shown in Figure 11F and G.

claim: G3BP1 functions to enhance norovirus VPg-dependent translation initiation.
source: These data further confirm that G3BP1 functions to enhance norovirus VPg-dependent translation initiation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro translation data showing reduced translation in the absence of G3BP1.

claim: G3BP1 plays a key role in the processes of norovirus VPg-dependent protein synthesis.
source: Furthermore, we determined that G3BP1 plays a key role in the processes of norovirus VPg-dependent protein synthesis, uncovering a new function for G3BP1 in facilitating RNA virus genome translation.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The combined approaches resulted in the identification of the core stress granule component G3BP1 as a host protein critical for the replication of both murine and human noroviruses in cell culture.
source: Our combined approaches resulted in the identification of the core stress granule component G3BP1 as a host protein critical for the replication of both murine and human noroviruses in cell culture.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion drawn from all three experimental approaches (proteomics and CRISPR) and validation experiments.

claim: Feline calicivirus (FCV) cleaves G3BP1 to inhibit stress granule formation.
source: Furthermore, we have previously shown that feline calicivirus (FCV), a relative of noroviruses within the Vesivirus genus, cleaves G3BP1 to inhibit stress granule formation (Humoud et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: MNV infection does not result in G3BP1 cleavage and instead forms cytoplasmic foci the composition of which is distinct from canonical stress granules.
source: In contrast, MNV infection does not result in G3BP1 cleavage and instead forms cytoplasmic foci the composition of which is distinct from canonical stress granules (Brocard et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: G3BP1 is one member of a group of G3BP proteins that possess RNA binding activity and have multiple cellular functions including the regulation of RNA stability and translation in response to stress.
source: G3BP1 is one member of a group of G3BP proteins (Ras-GTPase-activating protein (SH3 domain)-binding proteins), referred to as Rasputin in insects, that possess RNA binding activity and have multiple cellular functions including the regulation of RNA stability and translation in response to stress.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about G3BP proteins.

claim: G3BPs play a role in cancer cell survival, cancer metastasis and invasion, processing of specific miRNAs and stress granule formation.
source: It is now well accepted that G3BPs play a role in cancer cell survival, cancer metastasis and invasion, processing of specific miRNAs and stress granule formation (Reviewed in Alam and Kennedy, 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and cites a review article.

claim: Stress granules are dynamic cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein complexes that form rapidly under stress conditions and within which cellular RNAs are stored in stalled translation complexes.
source: Stress granules are dynamic cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein complexes that form rapidly under stress conditions and within which cellular RNAs are stored in stalled translation complexes (Protter and Parker, 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and cites a reference.

claim: The formation of cytoplasmic stress granules is part of the anti-viral defense mechanism.
source: In the context of viral infection, numerous studies have suggested that many, if not all, viruses must interact in some manner with stress granules as there is growing evidence that the formation of cytoplasmic stress granules is part of the anti-viral defense mechanism (Reviewed in McCormick and Khaperskyy, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and cites a review article.

claim: Some viruses interact with stress granules to promote viral replication.
source: Some viruses interact with stress granules to promote viral replication (Cristea et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2016; Panas et al., 2014; Panas et al., 2012) whereas some do so to counteract the inhibitory effect of stress granules on the translation of viral RNA (Panas et al., 2015; White et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on virus-stress granule interactions.

claim: Some viruses interact with stress granules to counteract the inhibitory effect of stress granules on the translation of viral RNA.
source: Some viruses interact with stress granules to promote viral replication (Cristea et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2016; Panas et al., 2014; Panas et al., 2012) whereas some do so to counteract the inhibitory effect of stress granules on the translation of viral RNA (Panas et al., 2015; White et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on virus-stress granule interactions.

claim: G3BP1 plays a key role in promoting the translation of norovirus VPg-linked viral RNA.
source: Our data suggests that G3BP1 plays a key role in promoting the translation of norovirus VPg-linked viral RNA.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Positive sense RNA viruses have evolved mechanisms to ensure the efficient translation of their viral genomic RNAs in the presence of high concentrations of competing cellular RNAs.
source: Positive sense RNA viruses have evolved mechanisms to ensure the efficient translation of their viral genomic RNAs in the presence of high concentrations of competing cellular RNAs.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about positive sense RNA virus translation strategies.

claim: The RGG motif of G3BP1 is essential for the association between G3BP1 and 40S subunits as well as the ability to form stress granules.
source: The RGG motif of G3BP1 is known to be essential for the association between G3BP1 and 40S subunits as well as the ability to from stress granules, whereas data would suggest that the RRM may play a regulatory role (Kedersha et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and cites a reference.

claim: The RRM domain of G3BP1 may play a regulatory role.
source: The RGG motif of G3BP1 is known to be essential for the association between G3BP1 and 40S subunits as well as the ability to from stress granules, whereas data would suggest that the RRM may play a regulatory role (Kedersha et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and cites a reference.

claim: The RGG and RRM domains were required for the function of G3BP1 in the norovirus life cycle.
source: These domains were also required for the function of G3BP1 in the norovirus life cycle (Figure 6) confirming that the G3BP1 association with 40S is important for its role in promoting norovirus VPg-dependent translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by complementation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The G3BP1 association with 40S is important for its role in promoting norovirus VPg-dependent translation.
source: These domains were also required for the function of G3BP1 in the norovirus life cycle (Figure 6) confirming that the G3BP1 association with 40S is important for its role in promoting norovirus VPg-dependent translation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the complementation experiments showing that RNA binding domains are required for G3BP1 function.

claim: RGG domains have many functions.
source: Importantly, RGG domains are known to have many functions (Thandapani et al., 2013) and therefore in the context of G3BP1 function in the norovirus life cycle, may also contribute to unknown interactions that promote norovirus translation.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and cites a reference.

claim: In the context of G3BP1 function in the norovirus life cycle, the RGG domain may contribute to unknown interactions that promote norovirus translation.
source: Importantly, RGG domains are known to have many functions (Thandapani et al., 2013) and therefore in the context of G3BP1 function in the norovirus life cycle, may also contribute to unknown interactions that promote norovirus translation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting possible additional functions of the RGG domain beyond 40S binding.

claim: G3BP1 is sequestered by binding to the nsP3 protein in alphaviruses.
source: Previous work on alphaviruses have shown that G3BP1 is sequestered by binding to the nsP3 protein (Panas et al., 2012; Panas et al., 2014; Panas et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on alphavirus-G3BP1 interactions.

claim: The alphavirus nsP3-G3BP1 interaction occurs via an FGDF motif also found in other viral proteins including the ICP8 protein of herpes simplex virus.
source: Furthermore, this interaction occurs via an FGDF motif also found in other viral proteins including the ICP8 protein of herpes simplex virus (Panas et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on viral protein-G3BP1 interaction motifs.

claim: The MNV VPg protein has a similar motif FGDGF to the FGDF motif found in alphavirus nsP3.
source: While the MNV VPg protein has a similar motif FGDGF (Figure 1A), this motif is not conserved in the GI Norwalk virus VPg protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The FGDGF motif is not conserved in the GI Norwalk virus VPg protein.
source: While the MNV VPg protein has a similar motif FGDGF (Figure 1A), this motif is not conserved in the GI Norwalk virus VPg protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The interaction of VPg with G3BP1 is not direct.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that the interaction of VPg with G3BP1 is not direct, fitting with our observation that this interaction is reduced by mutations in the eIF4G binding domain (Figure 1A and Figure 9B.)
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the lack of a conserved G3BP1 binding motif and the dependence on eIF4G binding.

claim: G3BP1 may make multiple contacts between the 40S subunit and viral RNA genome directly.
source: Recent studies have confirmed that G3BP1 is enriched at sites of viral RNA synthesis (Brocard et al., 2018; Fritzlar et al., 2019) so it is possible that G3BP1 makes multiple contacts between the 40S subunit and viral RNA genome directly.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting a possible mechanism for G3BP1 function.

claim: Additional contacts between G3BP1, 40S subunit, and viral RNA may further promote viral VPg-dependent translation and/or another aspect of the viral life cycle.
source: These additional contacts, may further promote viral VPg-dependent translation and/or another aspect of the viral life cycle.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting possible additional functions of G3BP1.

claim: BV2 murine microglial cells support the replication of the HuNoV GI replicon, albeit to a lesser degree than BHK or U20S cells.
source: Furthermore we were able to show that BV2 murine microglial cells support the replication of the HuNoV GI replicon, albeit it to a lesser degree than BHK or U20S cells (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: All the machinery necessary for HuNoV replication is conserved between human, hamster and mouse cells.
source: These data confirm that all the machinery necessary for HuNoV replication is conserved between human, hamster and mouse cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation that HuNoV can replicate in cells from different species.

claim: Reconstitution of the ΔG3BP1 BV2 microglial cells with WT G3BP1 at least partially restored the ability of the HuNoV GI replicon to form colonies.
source: Furthermore, reconstitution of the ΔG3BP1 BV2 microglial cells with WT G3BP1, at least partially restored the ability of the HuNoV GI replicon to form colonies, confirming the specificity of the effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Norovirus infection leads to preferential viral-translation whereby cellular mRNAs induced in response to norovirus infection are inefficiently translated.
source: We have previously found that norovirus infection leads to preferential viral-translation whereby cellular mRNAs induced in response to norovirus infection are inefficiently translated (Emmott et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The modification of host cell translation during norovirus infection is at least partially driven by the ability of the viral NS6 protease to cleave PABP and the induction of apoptosis which results in cleavage of cellular translation initiation factors.
source: This modification of host cell translation is at least partially driven by the ability of the viral NS6 protease to cleave PABP and the induction of apoptosis which results in cleavage of cellular translation initiation factors (Emmott et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Caspase cleaved translation initiation factors do not support host cell cap-dependent translation, but the cleaved forms of eIF4G do support norovirus VPg-dependent translation.
source: Importantly, whilst caspase cleaved translation initiation factors do not support host cell cap-dependent translation, we have previously found that the cleaved forms of eIF4G do support norovirus VPg-dependent translation (Emmott et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The ability of the norovirus protease to cleave PABP and other substrates is controlled by polyprotein processing and interactions with other viral proteins.
source: The ability of the norovirus protease to cleave PABP and other substrates is also controlled by polyprotein processing and interactions with other viral proteins (Emmott et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The preferential viral translation is not driven by the GCN2-mediated phosphorylation of eIF2α in MNV infected cells.
source: Recent work confirms that the preferential viral translation is not driven by the GCN2-mediated phosphorylation of eIF2α in MNV infected cells (Brocard et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: NS3 may contribute to the translational shut off seen in MNV infected cells.
source: We note however that others have suggested that NS3 may contribute to the translational shut off seen in MNV infected cells (Fritzlar et al., 2019), with the caveat that this observation was made outside of the context of infected cells and used overexpressed tagged viral proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to other work, but with caveats noted about the experimental system.

claim: Noroviruses use multiple mechanisms that work cooperatively to enable the control of host gene expression and the subsequent translation of the cellular mRNAs.
source: We suspect that noroviruses use multiple mechanisms that work cooperatively to enable the control of host gene expression and the subsequent translation of the cellular mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the various mechanisms described in the literature.

claim: The relative contribution of these processes in any given cell type may vary dependent on the degree to which the cells can sense and respond to viral infection through the induction of innate and apoptotic responses.
source: The relative contribution of these processes in any given cell type may also vary dependent on the degree to which the cells can sense and respond to viral infection through the induction of innate and apoptotic responses.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting variability in mechanisms across cell types.

claim: The viral proteins present in the viral translation complex may be distinct from those present in complexes active for viral RNA synthesis.
source: The observation that many of the factors enriched using the VPg protein were only enriched on complexes purified with NS1/2 tagged infectious MNV, could suggest that the viral proteins present in the viral translation complex are distinct from those present in complexes active for viral RNA synthesis.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the differential enrichment of factors with NS1/2 vs NS4.

claim: Unprocessed NS1/2 at the N-terminus of the ORF1 polyprotein being actively translated could function as an anchor, facilitating the enrichment of ribosomes and the associated factors.
source: However, we cannot formally rule out other possible explanations including the possibility that the specific enrichment of translation factors on NS1/2 occurs because NS1/2 is the first protein to be translated from ORF1, therefore unprocessed NS1/2 at the N-terminus of the ORF1 polyprotein being actively translated could function as an anchor, facilitating the enrichment of ribosomes and the associated factors.
evidence: The claim is an alternative hypothesis to explain the differential enrichment observed.

claim: VPg-containing precursors may bind the translation initiation factor eIF4G less well.
source: In addition, we have previously seen that VPg-containing precursors may bind the translation initiation factor eIF4G less well (Leen et al., 2016), which could prevent some VPg (NS5) containing precursors associating with translation initiation complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The norovirus replication complex contains a number of highly conserved viral protein-viral protein interactions.
source: Furthermore, the norovirus replication complex contains a number of highly conserved viral protein-viral protein interactions (Emmott et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Within the network of viral protein interactions, the NS1/2 protein interacts with the viral RNA polymerase NS7, which in turn binds VPg.
source: Within this network of interactions, the NS1/2 protein interacts with the viral RNA polymerase NS7, which in turn binds VPg.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about norovirus protein interactions.

claim: It is possible that the interactions observed between the NS1/2 proteins and the host proteins involved in translation occurs via the formation of a NS1/2-NS7-VPg complex.
source: It is therefore possible that the interactions observed between the NS1/2 proteins and the host proteins involved in translation, occurs via the formation of a NS1/2-NS7-VPg complex.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on known protein-protein interactions.

claim: Proteins involved in vesicle transport and lipid metabolism were significantly enriched in the replication complex, fitting with previous observations that the viral replication complex is associated with cytoplasmic membranous structures.
source: The high enrichment of proteins involved in vesicle-mediated transport, organelle organisation and exocytosis, fits well with our current understanding on the nature of the norovirus replication complex and the impact on host cell processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis and cites previous work on replication complex membrane association.

claim: The NS1/2 and NS4 proteins are thought to be key to the process of forming membrane-bound replication complexes.
source: The process by which the non-structural proteins induce the formation of these structures is unknown, but the NS1/2 and NS4 proteins are thought to be key to the process.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about norovirus replication complex formation.

claim: The norovirus NS4 protein associates with lipid droplets and is able to drive the formation of SMVs and DMVs.
source: The norovirus NS4 protein associates with lipid droplets and is able to drive the formation of SMVs and DMVs (Doerflinger et al., 2017), suggesting that it may regulate the biosynthetic pathways involved in lipid synthesis or intracellular vesicular transport pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work and includes an inference about NS4 function.

claim: NS4 may regulate the biosynthetic pathways involved in lipid synthesis or intracellular vesicular transport pathways.
source: The norovirus NS4 protein associates with lipid droplets and is able to drive the formation of SMVs and DMVs (Doerflinger et al., 2017), suggesting that it may regulate the biosynthetic pathways involved in lipid synthesis or intracellular vesicular transport pathways.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the known functions of NS4.

claim: The characterisation of the replication complex indicates an intimate link with numerous proteins involved in vesicle transport and lipid metabolism.
source: Our characterisation of the replication complex indicates an intimate link with numerous proteins involved in vesicle transport and lipid metabolism (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry and gene ontology data.

claim: NS1/2 and NS4 likely work in concert to drive the formation of membrane-bound replication complex by regulating the functions of multiple components.
source: Given that NS1/2 and NS4 interact to form a complex (Emmott et al., 2019), it is likely they work in concert to drive the formation of membrane-bound replication complex by regulating the functions of multiple components, the characterisation of which will require further analysis.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on known protein interactions and the proteomic data.

claim: G3BP1 is a host protein that has a critical role in the life cycle of murine and human noroviruses.
source: We identify G3BP1 as a host protein that has a critical role in the life cycle of murine and human noroviruses, identifying the first cellular pro-viral protein with pan-norovirus activity.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: G3BP1 is the first cellular pro-viral protein with pan-norovirus activity.
source: We identify G3BP1 as a host protein that has a critical role in the life cycle of murine and human noroviruses, identifying the first cellular pro-viral protein with pan-norovirus activity.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion drawn from the observation that G3BP1 is required for both MNV and HuNoV replication.

claim: Targeting G3BP1 may hold future therapeutic potential.
source: Furthermore, given the apparent importance of G3BP1 to an early stage of the norovirus life cycle, this work suggests that targeting G3BP1 may hold future therapeutic potential.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting a potential therapeutic application based on the findings.
